menu.term: Menu Economics: Food Cost, Yield & Par
menu.definition: FOOD COST %: ingredient cost ÷ menu price, the industry's heartbeat, typically targeted 25–35%, but CONTRIBUTION MARGIN (dollars left per plate) pays rent, not percentages: a 40% pasta earning $6 beats a 20% garnish earning $2. YIELD: usable product after trim and cooking: a $12/kg fish at 45% yield is really $26/kg on the plate; costing raw invoice prices is the classic rookie bankruptcy. PAR LEVELS: the standing quantity each ingredient is stocked to, driving daily orders. MENU ENGINEERING sorts items by popularity × profit (stars, plowhorses, puzzles, dogs) and edits accordingly. PRIX FIXE and TASTING MENUS trade choice for kitchen efficiency and predictable cost. The dish is art; the menu is a spreadsheet wearing art's clothes — a restaurateur must love both.

prime.term: Prime Cost: The Number That Runs the Building
prime.definition: COGS + TOTAL LABOR = PRIME COST, the two controllable giants, combined into the single metric operators live by: target 55–60% of sales for full service (under 55% is excellent; over 65% is a countdown). Why combined: the two trade against each other: house-made everything raises labor and lowers COGS; convenience products reverse it; scratch bread at a bakery-café and bought bread at a steakhouse can both be RIGHT, and prime cost is the referee that doesn't care which lever you pulled, only what they sum to. The management cadence: calculate it WEEKLY (the KPI entry's dashboard), not just at month-end: weekly prime cost turns a bleeding month into a bleeding week, caught while schedules and orders can still change. The decomposition when it's high: COGS side — pricing, portioning, waste, theft, vendor creep (their entries); labor side — scheduling to forecast, overtime leaks, over-staffed slow dayparts (its entry). One number, reviewed relentlessly, explains more restaurant survival than any other figure in this module.

cogs.definition: Where percentage points hide. THE SYSTEM: standardized recipes (the spec entry's kitchen twin: the 200th plate costs what the 2nd did), portion tools in use (scales, ladles, ramekins; eyeballing is a rounding error you pay for hourly), receiving discipline (weigh and count deliveries against invoices; short cases and thumb-on-scale vendors are a real tax), FIFO storage (the food-safety entry, monetized), and waste logs (what died in the walk-in, and why; over-prepping is the most common villain). THE MATH: physical inventory weekly or per-period → ACTUAL COGS = beginning + purchases − ending; compare against THEORETICAL COGS (what the POS says you sold, costed by recipe); the VARIANCE between them is your leak meter: waste, portioning drift, unrecorded comps, or theft. THEFT, named honestly: industry estimates run 3–5% of revenue across skimming, unrung sales, over-pouring for tips (the bar entry's audit), and back-door product. The answers are systems, not suspicion: POS controls, manager-only voids, camera-visible registers, and inventory variance reviewed with the team openly. Culture note: the goal is a kitchen where numbers are everyone's craft pride, not a surveillance state — the chef who knows their food cost to the tenth is displaying knife skills of a different kind.

pricing.definition: The menu-engineering entry's sequel: setting the numbers themselves. THE FLOOR: cost every recipe (the scale entry's grams make this possible) and price to target margin, but remember the CONTRIBUTION lesson: percentage is vanity, dollars pay rent (the $6-margin pasta beats the $2-margin salad at any percentage). THE PSYCHOLOGY, used ethically: charm-price endings ($18 vs $19 reads bigger than a dollar; whole numbers signal fine dining), NO dollar signs or price columns (prices nested after descriptions, not aligned for comparison shopping), ANCHORING (one premium item makes neighbors reasonable: the wine list entry's architecture, plated), decoy items, and description quality (provenance and technique words measurably lift both orders and price tolerance: 'Gulf shrimp, chargrilled' outsells 'shrimp'). THE MAINTENANCE: reprice quarterly against invoice creep (vendor increases arrive silently; menus that sleep bleed), engineer seasonally (the seasonality entry's food-cost gift), and take increases in small regular steps; guests forgive 3% annually and revolt at 15% once. The confidence rule: price for the value you deliver, not your imposter syndrome; underpricing is the quietest, most common form of restaurant self-harm.

bands.label: Prime cost

quadrants.label: Star
quadrants.advice: Protect it. Do not touch the recipe, the price, or its place on the page.

quadrants.label: Plowhorse
quadrants.advice: Sells well and earns little. Cut cost or nudge price: never both at once.

quadrants.label: Puzzle
quadrants.advice: Earns well and nobody orders it. Rename, redescribe, or move it up the page.

quadrants.label: Dog
quadrants.advice: Neither sells nor earns. Cut it, unless it is there for a reason you can name.
